overview: The Azande formed several connected kingdoms in central Africa. This record’s 900 to 1000 dates and enormous outline are unreliable for those states: the histories discussed here concern the much later kingdoms and their communities. The evidence does not establish a medieval Azande empire.

periods.title: Documented nineteenth-century kingdoms
periods.summary: Avungara rulers expanded from the Mbomu valley; Gbudwe’s kingdom ended under colonial attack in 1905. This is historical context outside the imported interval.

periods.title: Community life under colonial rule
periods.summary: Older ruling families remained, while colonial authorities reorganized political institutions and settlements.

sections.title: Several kingdoms, not one medieval empire

items.text: Nineteenth-century Azande rulers belonged to the Avongara aristocracy. Kings appointed governors to smaller areas, and princes could fight over succession. Political connections did not make every Zande community part of a single centralized state.

In the first half of the nineteenth century, Zande expansion crossed the Congo-Nile watershed from the Mbomu valley. Gbudwe established a kingdom around Yambio while confronting slave traders and neighboring powers.

Colonial borders divided Zande lands among Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, French Equatorial Africa and the Belgian Congo. Communities and ruling families survived those partitions, but their political autonomy and connections were profoundly disrupted.

A photograph from Yambio, taken between 1927 and 1930, shows a large soro granary reached by a ladder. Grain was stored upstairs; woven reeds or grass enclosed additional storage below. This family’s pantry had its own upper floor.

In another Yambio photograph from 1927 to 1930, women sit together beating finger millet with sticks. The grain supplied porridge and beer. Preparing food could be a shared task long before it reached a cooking pot.

A potter photographed between 1927 and 1930 stands beside coil-built earthenware vessels used in everyday life. Evans-Pritchard admitted that learning pottery from Zande men went badly for him. Expertise did not transfer just because the visitor owned a notebook.

A 1927 photograph records wives and children in Prince Rikita’s homestead, with crops beside the approach and houses behind them. This is a particular aristocratic family, showing how a royal lineage continued after Gbudwe’s defeat.

The game abanga could use a carved board or holes in the earth. A photograph dated 1927 to 1930 shows the ground version tucked under a hut’s eaves, with a stool ready nearby. No game box was required.

A kundi harp collected between 1927 and 1930 has five strings, wooden tuning pegs and a hide-covered soundbox. Plant materials form the strings and their attachments. Musicians and makers combined different natural materials to control tension and sound.

Colonial schooling could mix instruction with coercion. At Wau’s technical school, established in 1905 to teach carpentry, reading and writing, Rikita’s son Rumba was among pupils held as guarantees of their families’ submission.

A Zande written sample is “Rikita ni-fu-re na kporo.” The researchers translate it as “Rikita gave me a district to administer.” Published in their 2011 study, it comes from a historical narrative published in 1963, using a modern Latin-script transcription.

When researchers shared these older recorded stories with Zande speakers in Bangassou, participants wanted copies to take home. Language research could also return accounts of ancestors and political life to people whose heritage the stories preserved.

ending.text: Gbudwe was killed in 1905 and colonial rule replaced autonomous kingship. In 2022, a new Azande monarchy was established within South Sudan, combining four historical kingdoms as a modern institution. It was not a return of their former sovereign powers.
